In the USA the use of adjuvant tamoxifen is also suggest- ed,3-5 but studies have produced conflicting reports of ben- efit on recurrence,5,7 and again, there is no proven effect on survival; French guidelines suggest that the use of adju- vant hormonal therapy be confined to clinical trials.6 Ad- juvant use of newer oestrogen modulators such as anastro- zole is also under investigation.5,7 In patients with early disease (stage I or II; a relatively small tumour with no or limited nodal involvement) the prognosis is fairly good. Primary treatment is surgical.1,3,9 Breast-conserving surgery followed by postoperative radi- otherapy has been shown to have equivalent local recur- rence rates and 10-year survival (about 60%) to mastecto- my.10 The use of postoperative radiotherapy after breast- conserving surgery reduces local recurrence rates, but does not appear to affect overall survival.10,11 Radiotherapy is not usually used after mastectomy, but there are some stud- ies indicating that it may have additional benefits in pa- tients at high risk of recurrence.12,13 Further adjuvant therapy with cytotoxic chemotherapy or hormonal manipulations such as tamoxifen and ovarian ablation by surgery, radiotherapy, or gonadorelin ana- logues has been given to try to eradicate the micrometas- tases which cause relapses. Overviews of a large number of trials by the Early Breast Cancer Trialists’ Collaborative Group (EBCTCG) have confirmed the benefits of adju- vant therapy and attempted to determine which women de- rive most benefit and which regimens are most effec- tive.14-18 Analyses from these18 and the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project (NSABP) B-14 and B- 20 trials19 permitting up to 15 years of follow-up have shown that: • all women with early-stage breast cancer benefit from adjuvant therapy (although the size of the benefit varies) • the benefit continues to increase with time, suggesting that adjuvant therapy is curative in a proportion of wom- en who would otherwise relapse • about 6 months of anthracycline-based chemotherapy reduces the annual death rate due to breast cancer by about 38% in women under 50 years of age at diagnosis, and about 20% in those aged 50 to 69 at diagnosis (too few women over 70 were given chemotherapy to esti- mate benefit in this group) • this survival advantage occurs largely independent of oestrogen receptor (ER) status, nodal status, or other tu- mour characteristics • adjuvant regimens including an anthracycline are more effective than those without a drug of this class • in women with ER-positive disease, about 5 years of treatment with adjuvant tamoxifen reduces the annual death rate due to breast cancer by around 31%, largely independent of age, other tumour characteristics, or the use of chemotherapy • combined chemotherapy and
